rv.q: New shoots keep growing from Tim Crouch’s An Oak Tree , its legend quietly bubbling away for 20 years and its strange, unsettling magnificence never wavering. First performed in 2005, it was a solid rejection of stuffy plays where the actors say their memorised words each night in the same way.
If you get lucky, you are in for an absolute treat.
As with the Michael Craig-Martin artwork it references, I can admire the concept and the artistry of the piece, while not entirely connecting to it on an emotional level.

The audience is taken from the awkward, giggling, fear of the unknown to seeing a father’s grief unlocked on stage and you feel safe in knowing that all reactions and thoughts from the actor are genuine, provoking real heartfelt reactions from the audience too.
An unusual, funny, and surprisingly moving production that's well worth experiencing.

Tim Crouch's theatrical experiment still holds weight, and that even the sceptics among us (me) can appreciate the way form and structure are played with, twisted, and occasionally abandoned altogether.
Yet while I respected An Oak Tree, I rarely felt emotionally invested in it.
The more fascinating the theatrical experiment becomes, the harder it is to engage with the human story at its centre.

cn.t: Crouch's experimental two-hander, featuring a rotating cast of unprepared guests, remains a strange and revelatory exploration of grief and theatrical illusion 20 years on, though its conceptual ambitions don't always fully land.
